title: Individual fishing quota

definition.text: Individual fishing quotas, also called individual transferable quotas, are catch shares: a regulator sets a total allowable catch and hands portions of it to individual fishers.

facts.text: The total allowable catch is set per species, usually by weight and for a given period.
Quotas can usually be bought, sold and leased, a feature called transferability.
As of 2008, 148 major fisheries had adopted some form of the approach, and about 10% of the marine harvest was managed by ITQs.
The Netherlands, Iceland and Canada adopted them first in the late 1970s; New Zealand made ITQs national policy in 1986.
Like pollution quotas, ITQs are a cap-and-trade approach, but they regulate the industry's actual product rather than a by-product.
A 2008 study of 11,000 fisheries found catch share fisheries only half as likely to fail as open-access ones, nearly a third of which had collapsed.
Compared with other modern management schemes, however, IFQ fisheries show no long-term ecological advantage.
Alaska's halibut season, cut to two or three days before ITQs in 1995, now lasts nearly eight months.

contested_note: Studies disagree on whether IFQs improve stock health, and critics fault their social effects on small-scale fishers.

title: Rule of capture
article: Individual fishing quota#A move to privatisation and market-based mechanisms

definition.text: The rule of capture means a fisher owns a fish only once it is caught, which economists see as the main driver of overfishing.

facts.text: It encourages competitive racing and over-investment in boats and gear.
Without a long-term right to the stock, no one has a reason to conserve fish for the future.
Each boat plays a zero-sum game: any fish it leaves will likely be taken by another boat.

definition.text: The race to fish is the scramble to catch as much as possible during short open seasons, which catch shares are designed to end.

facts.text: Early management set a fishing season whose length tracked how abundant the stock was.
With catch shares, fishers can schedule trips as they like, boom-and-bust market cycles fade, and fishing in hazardous weather becomes unnecessary.

title: Quota allocation: grants versus auctions

definition.text: Fishing quotas can first be handed out free, usually by past catch, or sold at auction, and the choice decides who captures the resource's value.

facts.text: Grants by catch history give individuals a valuable right at no cost and are inherently political.
Auctions repay the public for access, like US radio spectrum auctions that raised tens of billions of dollars.
Russia's 2019 crab quota auction raised about 2 billion euro.
In Iceland critics argue quotas should be returned to the state and auctioned so the public gets a fair share of profits.

contested_note: Whether quotas should be granted to incumbents or auctioned is a live political dispute, notably in Iceland.

title: Criticisms of individual fishing quotas

definition.text: Critics say individual fishing quotas privatise a public resource, concentrate it in few hands and hurt fishing communities.

facts.text: First recipients get windfall profits, while later entrants must buy or lease the right to fish.
About eight companies control 80% of New Zealand's fisheries through quota purchases.
Bering Sea crab lease fees can reach 80% of landed value, leaving active fishers 20% of revenue.
Leasing gives rise to 'armchair fishermen' who hold quota but do not fish.

contested_note: Supporters credit IFQs with preventing collapses; critics stress consolidation, job loss and harm to coastal communities.

definition.text: Highgrading is catching more fish than a quota allows and dumping the less valuable ones so that the quota is filled with the best fish.

facts.text: Many dumped fish are already dead or die soon, adding to the drain on stocks.
ITQs can change the criteria fishers use to decide which fish to keep.

definition.text: A marine protected area (MPA) is a protected part of the seas, oceans or estuaries where human activity is restricted for conservation.

facts.text: Rules vary widely, covering development, fishing methods, seasons, catch limits and bans on disturbing marine life.
Not all MPAs are no-take zones: less than 1 percent of US waters are no-take.
Meta-analyses show no-take reserves give the biggest ecological benefits, largest when well-monitored, over ten years old and suitably sized.
Biodiversity in fully protected MPAs rose by an average of 23% after designation.
MPAs can support fishing through stock recovery and create jobs through ecotourism; a 2024 meta-analysis found no net cost to fisheries across 24 countries.
In 2020 only about 7.5 to 8% of the global ocean was under a conservation designation.
Some MPAs are criticised by indigenous peoples for impinging on their land-use rights.

definition.text: Spillover is the net movement of fish, eggs and larvae from a recovering marine protected area into the fishing grounds around it.

facts.text: A 2020 meta-analysis of 23 fully protected areas found commercial species up to 80% more abundant inside, and biomass 54% higher near boundaries than farther away.
It sustains fishing nearby without extracting anything inside the reserve; such benefits are well documented worldwide.
Coastal MPAs are increasingly recognised by scientists and small-scale fishers as raising the density and size of commercial species in local waters.

title: Displaced fishing effort

definition.text: Displaced fishing effort is the worry that closing an area to fishing just pushes the same fishing elsewhere, cancelling the reserve's benefits.

facts.text: Studies accounting for displacement suggest MPAs can still yield a net biodiversity gain when sensitive species are present.
Displacement can still raise costs for fishers.

contested_note: Fisheries scientists dispute whether no-take MPAs benefit biodiversity once displaced effort is counted.
